About our statement
Our statement has been developed under the requirements of the Aotearoa New Zealand 
Climate Standards CS1, CS2 and CS3 (Standards). 
This statement has been prepared by the New Zealand branch of QBE Insurance (Australia) 
Limited (QBE New Zealand). We have used the framework provided by the Standards to consider 
and provide information about the climate change-related risks and opportunities to our activities. 
As our second year of full disclosure under these Standards: QBE New Zealand has chosen 
to use the following adoption provisions available within the CS2
•	 Adoption provision 2: Anticipated financial impacts.
•	 Adoption provision 4: Scope 3 Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions. 
•	 Adoption provision 7: Analysis of trends.
•	 Adoption provision 8: Scope 3 GHG emissions assurance. 
•	 Adoption of the exemption: Scope 3 emissions No Action under section 9(1)(a)(v) 
of the Financial Markets Authority Act 2011.
About this report
This is the Disclosure for QBE Insurance (Australia) Limited (and its subsidiaries) for the year ended 
31 December 2024, in respect of its New Zealand business. 
QBE Insurance Group Limited is the ultimate parent company of QBE Insurance (Australia) Limited (QIA). 
QBE Insurance Group Limited (Group) is headquartered in Sydney and listed on the Australian 
Securities Exchange.

Governance
Governance Oversight
QBE’s Group Board is responsible for the 
oversight of climate-related risks and 
opportunities that have the potential to impact 
QBE. It also oversees the sustainability impact 
of the Group’s activities and operations and sets 
standards on the Group’s environmental, social 
and governance responsibilities and practices.
The Group Board considers material risks to our business 
when approving and overseeing the implementation of QBE’s 
strategy, including the climate-related targets set out in the 
Sustainability Scorecard. The Group Board approves the 
Scorecard setting out the initiatives and targets designed to 
advance our sustainability strategy, including climate-related 
targets. Our sustainability strategy includes three focus 
areas: foster an orderly and inclusive transition to a net-zero 
economy, enable a sustainable and resilient workforce, 
and partner for growth through innovative, sustainable 
and impactful solutions. Progress against targets is monitored 
by the Group Board quarterly via reports, and progress 
is published annually as part of QBE Group’s annual reporting. 
In addition, the Group Board receives regular updates on our 
sustainability strategy and progress, including climate-related 
matters, from Group Sustainability; as well as risk updates 
from the Group Board Risk and Capital Committee (BRCC).
The Group Board is assisted in its oversight by 
committees composed of a majority of independent 
directors. In particular, the Board committees outlined 
on pages 4–5 have oversight responsibilities relating to 
climate-related matters.
The Board and committees' responsibilities in relation 
to climate-related risks and opportunities are set out in 
the Board and committee charters which are available at 
http://www.qbe.com/investor-relations/corporate-governance/
qbe-charters-and-constitution.
While the Group Board has ultimate oversight, the Group 
Board Audit Committee has responsibility for overseeing 
the effectiveness of QBE Group’s financial and sustainability 
reporting and risk management framework. In addition, 
the BRCC considers climate risk from a risk and capital 
management perspective. The BRCC is responsible for 
the oversight of all risks, including climate-related risks. 
Both committees support and make recommendations 
to the Group Board.
Skills and competencies
The Group Board has a skills matrix covering the range 
of competencies and experience of each director, 
including sustainability. The Board skills matrix is disclosed on 
pages 6–7 of QBE Group’s Corporate Governance Statement. 
Company structure
QBE Insurance Group Limited (QBE or Group), 
headquartered in Australia, is an international 
insurer and reinsurer offering a diverse portfolio 
of commercial, casualty and specialty products, 
personal lines and risk management solutions. 
QBE’s diverse product portfolio includes 
property, motor, crop, public and product liability, 
professional indemnity, workers’ compensation, 
energy, marine and aviation. We operate across 
three divisions: North America, Australia Pacific 
(AUSPAC) and International.
QBE is the ultimate parent company of QBE 
Insurance (Australia) Limited (QIA), which is one 
of the legal entities operating QBE’s AUSPAC 
division. The New Zealand business is a branch 
of QIA. AUSPAC has operations in Australia, 
New Zealand and across the Pacific including 
Fiji, French Polynesia, New Caledonia and the 
Solomon Islands. The distribution model varies 
between each country, as do the products. 
The New Zealand branch is managed by a CEO 
and Managing Director (MD), responsible for 
the New Zealand and Pacific Island branches. 
We are an intermediated insurer within the 
New Zealand market, and sell the following 
products including commercial motor, contract 
works and engineering, liability, marine, property, 
and trade credit.
The board of QBE Insurance Group Limited 
(Group Board) is the ultimate governing body of the 
QBE Group. The board of QBE Insurance (Australia) 
Limited (QIA Board) has oversight of AUSPAC, 
which includes New Zealand.

Divisional governance 
The role of the QIA Board is to provide guidance to and 
oversight of AUSPAC. This includes approving business

Executive and Management Oversight
The Group Executive Committee (GEC) is responsible 
for the management and execution of the Group’s 
strategic priorities, including managing climate-related 
risks and opportunities and overseeing the execution of 
QBE’s sustainability strategy and commitments. The CEO, 
AUSPAC, represents QBE New Zealand on the GEC and 
the Environmental and Social (E&S) GEC Sub-committee.
Sustainability and climate-related issues are managed 
through the Sustainability Design Forum, and the E&S 
Sub-committee. The E&S Sub-committee provide reports 
and updates to the GEC. In 2024, the Group Net Zero 
in Underwriting Steering Committee managed matters 
specific to underwriting as a sub-committee of the Group 
Underwriting Committee, which reports into the GEC. 
The AUSPAC Chief Underwriting Officer is a member of this 
Steering Committee. The composition of these committees 
are individuals with specialist knowledge in climate, 
sustainability and business functions including underwriting. 
The committees review and assess issues related to 
climate and make recommendations on actions to address 
climate-related risks and opportunities on a regular basis 
in line with their terms of reference.
The Executive Risk Committee, a sub-committee of the GEC, 
oversees all risks, including climate-related risk.
During 2024, the composition and responsibilities of the 
Sustainability management committees were reviewed 
following the issuance of mandatory climate-related disclosure 
requirements in Australia. The climate governance framework 
on pages 4–5 reflects the updated management committees 
that are in place as at 31 December 2024. The diagram also 
shows the frequency these committees meet, and how each 
provide oversight and interact with each other. Updates from 
these committees are presented to the Group Board by the 
representative Executive as appropriate.
Divisional Management 
In AUSPAC, the Executive Management Board (EMB) 
supports the progress of our global sustainability strategy 
and delivery of the initiatives and targets set out in our 
Sustainability Scorecard. The CEO and Managing Director 
for New Zealand and Pacific is a member of the EMB and 
reports to the CEO, AUSPAC, who is a member of the GEC.

Each NZPAC LT member is responsible for operationalising 
the businesses strategy and business plans, for their 
respective functional areas. In respect of assessing and 
managing climate-related risks and opportunities, this varies 
within each functional area. For example, our Head of Claims 
ensures business continuity plans are in place for a large-scale 
natural disaster. The GM Product and Underwriting for NZPAC 
maintains underwriting rules. Products are reviewed in 
accordance with the Product Governance Standard and the 
product team can add, remove or amend products with 
consideration to climate-related risks and/or opportunities. 
For example, construction insurance tailored for renewable 
energy projects. Our head of Actuarial and Analytics, 
considered technical pricing, which includes risk-based 
pricing for floods, as an example. As of 31 December 2024, 
there were 12 members of the NZPAC LT.
The Group Executive Corporate Affairs and Sustainability 
has executive level accountability for implementation 
of the QBE Group sustainability strategy, including oversight 
of our climate related commitments, which are embedded 
across the enterprise and owned by their respective GEC 
members. The Group Head of Sustainability reports directly 
to the Group Executive Corporate Affairs and Sustainability 
and is responsible for leading an integrated approach 
to sustainability. Working with key functional leaders to 
build capability and embed sustainability within business 
strategy and decision–making, this role manages a team 
of sustainability specialists including a Head of Climate. 
The Head of Climate is responsible for development 
and delivery of QBE’s climate strategy and the development 
of a transition plan. In addition, climate-related responsibilities 
are integrated into functional roles across the business.

Strategy
QBE continues to consider and respond to climate-related risks 
and opportunities through our sustainability strategy Focus Areas.
Business model and strategy
As one of the world’s largest insurance and reinsurance companies, with operations in all major insurance markets, 
there are a range of climate-related risks and opportunities that may impact our business, customers and the 
communities in which we operate over the short, medium and long term. Our response to climate-related risks 
and opportunities is part of our sustainability strategy, including initiatives driven by our sustainability Focus Areas. 
As of 31 December 2024, QBE’s six strategic priorities: portfolio optimisation, sustainable growth, bringing the 
enterprise together, modernise our business, our people, and customers help guide QBE New Zealand’s business 
strategy and annual business plans. 
Globally, QBE continues to work toward our commitments of a net-zero underwriting portfolio by 2050, a net-zero 
investment portfolio by 2050 and net zero in our own operations by 2030. In 2024, we commenced work to develop 
a Climate Transition Plan, which will be published in 2026. Our approach to managing our climate-related risks and 
opportunities is embedded in our sustainability strategy, specifically our Focus Area 1 – Foster an orderly and inclusive 
transition to a net-zero economy, and our Focus Area 3 – Partner for growth through innovative, sustainable and 
impactful solutions.

Operations 
In 2021, globally, QBE committed to net-zero operations 
by 2030 for our Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions, expanding this 
in 2022 to include material Scope 3 emissions. This was further 
refined in 2024 to a defined inventory of Scope 3 emissions 
relevant to our operations. The defined inventory, outlined in 
our Sustainability Data Book (Data Book), includes business 
travel, fuel- and energy-related activities and capital goods.
In New Zealand, we use 100% renewable electricity for our 
offices, and our fleet vehicles are either hybrid or electric. 
In 2024, we installed sensor lighting in our Auckland 
office to reduce electricity use and implemented a 
green waste option. 
Advocacy and Community
We share our experience and knowledge with the 
intention of stimulating investment to improve natural 
disaster resilience. In December 2024, our Group Head of 
Catastrophe Modelling Research co-authored an article 
published in IOP Science, titled 'Climate change impacts to 
extreme weather events associated with insured losses in 
New Zealand: a review'. This comprehensive review seeks 
to integrate and interpret the findings from a wide range 
of scientific literature into a cohesive summary useful for 
insurers evaluating climate risk in New Zealand. This review 
summarises the climate risk facing New Zealand, focusing 
on extreme events including heavy rainfall, floods, coastal 
hazards driven by weather systems, atmospheric rivers, 
ex- and extra-tropical cyclones and severe convective storms, 
as well as wildfire weather. Potential changes to natural 
climate variability are also considered.
As a member of the Insurance Council of New Zealand (ICNZ) 
and their Climate Change Committee, QBE New Zealand 
employees participate with the aim of promoting a responsive 
and sustainable insurance industry.
This year, QBE New Zealand supported climate mitigation 
efforts in the community where 43 employees participated 
in tree planting activities to support removal of carbon dioxide 
from the atmosphere. The participation was split between five 
charities, during an annual volunteer day organised by QBE 
New Zealand. Globally, we continue to support Red Cross and 
Save the Children through our Community Ready partnership 
which helps to enhance community resilience by preparing 
for, responding to and recovering from disasters.
Supply chain
In 2024, we published our Supplier Code of Responsible 
Conduct. This Code sets out QBE’s responsible conduct 
expectations and the key environmental, social and 
governance principles that we expect our suppliers to 
uphold when doing business with us.
Investments 
QBE’s Group Investments team manages investments 
on behalf of the Group. QBE seeks to responsibly invest 
our proprietary assets, including our premium income, 
across the globe. We have a commitment to align our 
investments portfolio to a net-zero economy and we aim 
to do this through target setting and tracking, scaling 
investments in climate solutions and engaging with external 
asset managers to influence the decarbonisation of their 
operations and funds under management. To measure 
our progress, we undertake climate-related analysis 
to assess our portfolio’s exposures to climate-related risks 
and opportunities and continue to evolve our coverage 
and approach as methodologies and solutions to data 
challenges become available.

Aligned with our broader climate strategy and our

QBE is committed to transitioning its investment portfolio

We have achieved our 2025 targets and are working on

Engagement 
As asset owners, we have a unique role at the top of the investment value chain, and we acknowledge both the 
responsibilities and opportunities that come with this role. We believe that we can deliver meaningful impact by engaging 
in conversation with our external asset managers to influence sustainable practices in the transition to net zero.
In 2024, globally we continued to engage with all our external managers and the top 20 highest emitters in our investment 
grade corporate credit portfolio. We engage with our external managers as part of an annual process, which involves 
the collection and review of information and supporting documentation to understand how climate-related risks and 
opportunities are considered within their investment management processes as well as how these are managed within 
their own organisation. For the top 20 highest emitters in our investment grade corporate credit portfolio, we refined 
our engagement approach this year to include questions that are more targeted and tailored to each issuer based on 
consideration of their public disclosures. Our engagement was aimed at understanding their emission reduction targets 
and plans for achieving those targets, as well as readiness for compliance with the upcoming IFRS S2 Climate-related 
Disclosures (or the equivalent AASB S2 standard in Australia).

Underwriting
We are progressing our net-zero underwriting strategy by seeking to understand and respond to the evolving needs 
and ambitions of our customers and the broader economy. This work is led by our Group Underwriting Committee under 
the guidance of the Group Chief Underwriting Officer. The Environmental and Social GEC Sub-committee has oversight of 
how this contributes to our progress towards our net-zero commitments.
This year, we have continued to focus on progressing the three important areas:
1.   Customer engagement and insights 
We continue to work towards our commitment of a net-zero underwriting portfolio by 2050, and working with our customers 
is key to achieving this goal. Our underwriting approach includes engaging with and monitoring the emissions management 
progress of our priority commercial customers. In New Zealand, we continue to engage with our priority commercial customers 
(nine in 2024). Discussing climate-related topics enables us to deepen our understanding of the anticipated impacts and the 
potential risks and opportunities our customers may be facing and how we can potentially support them.
2.   Innovative products and services 
Globally, our customers are facing increasingly interconnected and complex challenges, including heightened geopolitical 
risk and economic uncertainty. QBE continues to monitor these risks and opportunities to identify how we can support 
our customers through the transition. Decarbonisation of the energy system remains a key opportunity for our customers 
to decarbonise their businesses. For example, in New Zealand, we now offer contract works and business interruption insurance 
for renewable energy construction. Opportunities to support the transition are incorporated into our business plans for some of 
our key markets.
3.   Emissions modelling and tracking 
We remain focused on improving our data and reporting to inform transition planning decision making. Our ability 
to improve our data remains constrained by availability of methodologies and the absence of relevant enabling regulation 
in certain jurisdictions. We expect that over time, as climate-related disclosures come into effect across jurisdictions, we will 
see improvements in emissions data quality and availability; although challenges may remain for businesses outside of 
mandatory sustainability reporting scope.
Our progress
Customer engagement is on track, in line with our 2023-2025 Sustainability 
Scorecard target to undertake formal engagement with at least 50 priority commercial 
customers globally.
We continue to explore opportunities to support the transition, including enhancing 
existing and offering new products and services.
Progress in our three important areas helps us refine our underwriting strategy to support the transition.

The anticipated impacts of climate-related risks and opportunities 
QBE continues to consider and respond to climate-related risks and opportunities through our 
sustainability strategy Focus Areas. There are a range of climate-related risks and opportunities 
that may impact our business, customers and the communities in which we operate over the short, 
medium and long term.
Our approach to managing climate risk in underwriting
It is expected that climate change will increase the 
frequency and severity of weather-related natural 
catastrophes over the medium to long term. In the 
short term, it is difficult to distinguish the impact of 
climate change versus the normal variability in weather 
and natural catastrophes.
Our underwriting approach, implemented through the 
business planning process, aims to diversify and manage 
insurance risks accepted and reduce volatility of returns. 
Our approach to managing the impact of physical climate 
risks is supported by a number of features and processes, 
utilising specialist teams where appropriate, to help improve 
the reliability and consistency of our results. These include, 
but are not limited to, annual policy renewal, pricing, 
our underwriting appetite, the purchase of reinsurance, 
and leveraging our catastrophe modelling capabilities.
The evaluation of the impact is supported by our 
accumulations management process, including 
regular updates to natural perils models, monitoring of 
property accumulations across the portfolio to simulate 
weather‑related loss potential, budgeting, price setting, 
and the use of reinsurance to protect capital and reduce 
earnings volatility. Our analysis concludes that the impact 
of climate change will vary significantly across regions 
and type of catastrophes. 
The impacts of climate change are also considered 
as part of our approach to planning for catastrophe 
risks. Our catastrophe allowance is set and reported 
at a Group‑wide level. This allowance is established above 
the long-term average of our modelled catastrophe costs. 
In 2024, our Group catastrophe costs of USD 1,048 million 
were below the Group's allowance of USD 1,280 million. 
In 2025, our catastrophe allowance is USD 1,160 million.
Opportunities to support the transition are incorporated 
into our business plans for key markets through to 
2030. We outline our approach to managing climate risk 
in underwriting in the Climate-related Risks and Opportunities 
section of our Annual Report. Our underwriting approach, 
described in more detail below, is implemented through 
the business planning process. This approach aims to 
diversify and manage insurance risks accepted and reduce 
volatility of returns. 
Annual renewability 
As our insurance policies typically renew annually, we can 
continuously adjust our pricing or underwriting appetite.
Pricing
The Catastrophe Accumulation Management team 
provides technical catastrophe pricing for a large 
number of commercial property and engineering 
policies. Pricing factors are refreshed using the most 
up‑to‑date catastrophe models available, to reflect 
current catastrophe accumulations, reinsurance costs 
and required return on capital. 
Underwriting appetite
We continue to manage our property exposures 
given the exposure to physical climate risk which 
has the potential to impact our business.
Reinsurance
In the short term, we manage the volatility of natural 
catastrophe claims by purchasing a comprehensive 
catastrophe reinsurance program with long-standing high 
credit graded reinsurance partners. We also consider a wide 
range of event frequency scenarios in our capital planning.
Catastrophe modelling
QBE has a global Catastrophe Accumulation Management 
team and a Catastrophe Modelling Research team. 
The Catastrophe Modelling Research team provides in-house 
capability to validate and customise our models, including 
for potential impacts of climate change.

Current climate-related impacts
Physical Impacts
Climate change is one of several drivers of the increasing costs of natural disasters globally. This can create volatility in profitability 
particularly in portfolios where QBE helps to protect customers’ assets from extreme weather. Each year, we budget a catastrophe 
allowance based on our latest catastrophe modelling which allows for potential climate-change impacts. 
To better understand the potential impact of climate change on specific perils and regions, we have worked with external 
partners to analyse the scientific literature related to the potential impact of climate change on those perils and regions. 
The scope, scenarios and timeframes analysed are summarised on page 14. These scenarios do not represent forecasts of the 
impact of climate change but indicate the potential outcomes if the scenario occurs. Following our analysis, we recalibrated our 
catastrophe models to reflect the potential change indicated by scientific literature. This was done to determine the potential 
impact to net claims costs under each scenario. 
Furthermore, in 2024, we partnered with external experts to enhance our natural hazard modelling and pricing capabilities. 
For QBE New Zealand, the development and deployment of risk-based flood pricing models provides us more confidence 
in pricing, reducing the risk our policies are underpriced for the exposure underwritten. While there were expenses related to 
building and deploying these models during 2024, these costs were not material. 
We cannot accurately attribute financial impact to climate change or climate-related perils as our reinsurers do not provide an 
apportionment of reinsurance premiums associated with climate-related perils. However, given the benign year for weather-related 
catastrophe events in New Zealand, we have not seen any material physical or financial climate-related impacts in the New Zealand 
portfolio in 2024.
Transition impacts 
Transition risks result from the changes associated with the 
global shift towards a net-zero economy. Transition risks are 
broad in nature and can be difficult to quantify or model. 
For instance, regulatory, geopolitical and social pressures 
can create material impacts on the operations of a business, 
its reputation, and the value of its assets.
Our Environmental and Social Risk Framework outlines 
our underwriting approach to sensitive sectors, including 
those facing higher transition risk. Transition risk analysis at 
a sectoral level may support us in reviewing our underwriting 
strategy and portfolio mix. However, it remains a challenge 
to classify the Group’s underwriting data at a granular sectoral 
level. We continue to make investments in data, people and 
systems to allow us to better understand our underwriting 
exposure at a sectoral level. 
In 2024, QBE New Zealand has not observed material 
climate transition impacts to the underwriting portfolio.
Climate transition plan
QBE will publish its climate transition plan in 2026, 
as guided by our parent entity’s climate-related disclosure 
obligations under Australian legislation. In 2024, 
QBE commenced work to develop a Group-wide climate 
transition plan that can be implemented at a regional/local 
level as appropriate, to address local climate-related risks 
and opportunities. As one of the world’s largest insurance 
and reinsurance companies, with operations in all major 
insurance markets, this work is a significant undertaking 
and consistency in our approach to climate transition 
planning and climate-related disclosures is key.

QBE continues to mature our approach to climate risk management 
through integration with internal frameworks, policies and business activities.
Climate risk governance
In AUSPAC, our QIA Board Risk and Capital Committee oversees climate risk and is supported by the Executive Risk 
and Capital Committee at the management level.
Climate risk management
QBE manages climate risk as part of ESG risk, a sub-class of strategic risk in our Risk Management Strategy. 
Climate risk interacts with other material risk classes such as insurance and operational risk.
Identifying and assessing climate risks
QBE Group reviews its top risks at least annually. As part of this process, we identify risks which may impact the business 
and assess their potential impact and likelihood, in line with our Risk and Control Self-Assessment (RCSA) Standard. Climate risk 
continues to be one of the top risks for QBE Group. Climate-related risks are assessed in line with our process for assessing 
all risks and not prioritised relative to other risks.
The RCSA Standard risk rating scales are applied to quantitatively and qualitatively assess the likelihood and impact of climate 
risk and determine its materiality to QBE. This assessment includes consideration of the impact of mitigation activities on the 
underlying risk. Due to the nature of the risks materialising, we consider the potential impacts of climate over the short, 
medium and long term, aligned to our business planning cycle, net-zero commitments and scenario analysis.
Climate risk is identified where relevant as part of our RCSA process. In New Zealand, the RCSA details risks that are relevant 
to climate risk exposure through concentration or portfolio mix, pricing, and business disruption due to a major weather event. 
At a Group level we continue to develop our ESG risks and controls library to support climate risk embedment and ownership 
across the business.
We undertake scenario analysis to understand the potential future impact of physical, transition and liability climate risks 
predominantly on our underwriting and investment portfolios. The outcomes of these scenarios help to inform strategic

Managing and monitoring climate risks
Climate risk is managed and monitored in line with the three lines model. The first line being business ownership of the risks, 
across underwriting, investments, supply chain and operations. The second line is risk and compliance, with independent 
oversight, support and challenge functions. The third line is internal audit and independent assurance function. 
To support our climate risk management, QBE has several policies which apply to our own operations and to third parties 
we do business with, including our Group Environment Policy, Environmental and Social Risk Framework and Supplier Code 
of Responsible Conduct.
Climate and other ESG and sustainability-related topics require robust review to mitigate against incorrect information being 
released externally. Our greenwashing checklist and training module provide further guidance to employees to mitigate this risk.
Where necessary, function‑specific training is available to first line teams to support their understanding of climate change 
and QBE’s approach to risk management in business-as-usual activities.
Our ESG risk team, who form part of our second line function, review and challenge the management actions in place relating 
to our climate risk management such as our Sustainability Scorecard and Environmental and Social Risk Framework to enable 
effective implementation and monitoring. Second line also provides support to review risks and controls which relate to how 
we manage our internal and external climate risks and obligations. ESG risk management training continues to be available 
on a voluntary basis to all employees across the Group.
We continue to monitor climate key risk indicators through our Group ESG risk dashboard and are in the process of 
developing regional‑specific dashboards which provide an additional localised approach to our climate risk management.
Internal audit (third line) provides independent assurance over how we manage climate risk to ensure robust controls 
and governance processes are in place. This year, in Group, the internal controls assurance team supported first line teams 
with improving the robustness of their climate‑related controls to develop our climate risk management maturity.
Business continuity plans are another way we manage climate risks. In November 2024, QBE New Zealand, along with other

energy usage  
Description: Emissions related to energy used by employees working from home 
(WFH) – electricity and natural gas. To estimate these emissions, QBE conducts an 
annual employee survey (in 2024 the response rate was 32%) to gather information 
about employees working from home such as number of days working from home 
and usage of solar and green power. Although survey results can be affected by factors 
such as respondent inaccuracies, timing of survey, response size and non-response bias,

information for estimating work from home emissions.
Emissions are measured as:

WFH x average kWh per person per hour x IEA emission factor x adjustment factor. 
Where FTE includes permanent workers, fixed-term workers, casuals, temporary workers 
and contractors. The FTE with solar and energy has been taken directly from the survey 
results and has not been extrapolated across the population of FTE to maintain a 
conservative estimate for WFH renewable energy consumption.
iii.	 Estimated natural usage emissions: Total FTE per country as at 31 December 2024 x 
estimated number of hours WFH x average GJ per person per hour x IEA emission

Climate scenario limitations
Climate projections are uncertain and complex, and do not account for all possible future variables. Outputs are sensitive 
to temperature, emissions and socioeconomic assumptions used.
•	 Transition scenarios, unless specified, do not consider 
individual company commitments to transform business 
models and abate emissions but rather rely on observed 
financial and ESG data to model future performance. 
Data quality and company disclosure varies and therefore 
the analysis predominately relies on sector averages.
•	 Physical risks are expected to have societal effects, 
including on health, migration and conflict. Whilst these 
might cause indirect impacts on investors, these complex 
dynamics are not included in this type of analysis. 
•	 The physical impacts of climate change are uncertain 
and climate science is a constantly evolving field. 
Whilst the link between emissions and temperature 
is well understood, there is more uncertainty about 
localised impacts and about impacts on extreme weather.
•	 The modelling does not cover physical hazards where 
the link to climate change is less well understood or 
where impacts on commercial assets are limited.
•	 Estimated average physical impacts could obscure 
changing tail risks, such as changes in the impacts 
of rare floods or drought events. The modelling 
accounts for expected average annual damages 
and impacts from temperature rise on economies. 
Supply chain interruptions from physical risks are 
not covered in the standard modelling. Supply chain 
interruptions from physical hazards such as flooding 
or hurricanes, when individual one‑off events, are likely 
to be transitory, but could impact in-year earnings.
•	 Each climate scenario will have its own set of temperature, 
emissions and socioeconomic assumptions, and results 
will be sensitive to these.
•	 Results are sensitive to the assumption that the market 
is currently pricing equities (and thereby margin outlooks) 
based on a 'current policies, current climate' baseline. 
•	 The model does not account for carbon market 
hedging or company-specific contracting arrangements. 
While some companies use hedging instruments 
to mitigate risks from carbon pricing, and other 
companies use long-term contracts to lock in product 
prices and volumes (e.g. LNG producers); this data is 
not considered in the modelling.
